content.title: About
content.content: Wonton is a traditional Asian dish consisting of a thin dough wrapper filled with vegetables, mushrooms or tofu and deep‑fried until golden and crispy. The meat‑free version is popular among vegetarians and anyone looking for a light yet satisfying snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wontons originate from Chinese cuisine, where they are often called “fried dumplings”.
The dough is made from flour, water and sometimes egg, giving it elasticity and a crunchy texture after frying.
Across Asia, wontons are served with a variety of dipping sauces: soy, vinegar, chili, or aromatic ginger sauce.
Fried wontons are a common appetizer in sushi bars and Asian‑fusion restaurants.
Meat‑free wontons can be easily adapted with tofu, mushrooms, carrots, cabbage or soy crumble.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When fried in a modest amount of vegetable oil, wontons retain a moderate fat content, mostly polyunsaturated.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Tofu or soy‑based fillings provide a complete amino‑acid profile useful for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and soy ingredients contain thiamine, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetable fillings such as cabbage, carrots and mushrooms add fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain dough and the absence of added sugars make fried wontons suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu and soy crumble can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Traditional soy sauces are salty; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Frying oil concerns
items.content: Over‑frying can create trans fats; it’s best to fry at the right temperature with a small amount of oil.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Undercooked wontons may stay soft inside, affecting texture and increasing bacterial risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot with soy, vinegar, or chili dipping sauce. Wontons can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, soups, or packed in bento boxes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked wontons in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a separate bag – they retain flavor and crunch for up to 2 months. Re‑heat by pan‑frying or baking.
